title: 23 people, one shared birthday?
hook: 23 people in a room. What are the odds two share a birthday?

knows: a percentage as a chance out of 100

misconception: A shared birthday in a group of 23 is unlikely, because 23 is small next to 365. (The learner silently answers a different question: does someone share MY birthday?)
objective: The learner can explain that a match can happen in any pair, that the number of pairs grows much faster than the number of people (23 people make 253 pairs), and so a match among 23 is about a coin flip.

claims.text: Assuming 365 equally likely birthdays (ignoring 29 February), a group of 23 has about a 50.7% chance that at least two people share a birthday.
claims.source: 1 - (365*364*...*343)/365^23 = 0.5073. Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1, 3rd ed. (1968), ch. II.3.

claims.text: Under the same assumption, 23 is the smallest group size for which the chance of a shared birthday exceeds 50% (22 people give about 47.6%).
claims.source: Same product formula evaluated at n = 22 (0.4757) and n = 23 (0.5073). Feller (1968), ch. II.3.

claims.text: The chance that at least one of the other 22 people in a group of 23 shares your own birthday is only about 6%.
With 50 people the chance of a shared birthday is about 97%, and with 70 it is about 99.9%.
claims.source: Product formula at n = 50 (0.9704) and n = 70 (0.9992). Feller (1968), ch. II.3.

claims.text: Real birthdays are not spread perfectly evenly over the year; unevenness can only raise the chance of a shared birthday above the equal-days figure.
claims.source: D. M. Bloom (1973), 'A birthday problem', American Mathematical Monthly 80(10): 1141-1142; A. G. Munford (1977), 'A note on the uniformity assumption in the birthday problem', The American Statistician 31(3): 119.

claims.text: The rooms on the stage are drawn by a seeded random generator with every day equally likely, so the share of rooms with a match settles toward the exact chance as more rooms are drawn.
claims.source: Demo.tsx: seeded generator, uniform over 365 days; law of large numbers.

claims.text: In a class of 30, the chance that some two share a birthday is about 71% (435 pairs).
For most people the first guess at the chance of a shared birthday among 23 people is far below the true 50.7%.
claims.source: v2: the sentence "far more than most people guess" was removed from the reveal (fact-check F2: no source for what people guess). Nothing learner-visible depends on this claim now. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Confirmed withdrawn: no 'most people guess' sentence on the stage.

claims.text: Each new person makes a pair with everyone already in the room: going from n to n + 1 people adds n new pairs.
claims.source: n(n+1)/2 - n(n-1)/2 = n; e.g. 22 -> 23 people adds 22 pairs (231 -> 253). Reveal v2: "Each new person makes a pair with everyone already there."

claims.text: People tend to answer a different question, "does anyone share my birthday?", whose answer is only about 6%, when asked about a shared birthday in a group.
claims.source: v2: "The trap is asking..." (a claim about how people reason) was replaced by "Compare a different question: does anyone share my birthday? Only about 6%", which asserts only c4. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Confirmed withdrawn: the reveal now says 'Compare a different question ... Only about 6%' with no claim about how people reason.

claims.text: If each of the 253 pairs in a group of 23 is treated as a separate 1-in-365 chance of a match, the chance that every pair misses is about 50%.
claims.source: (364/365)^253 = 0.4995. This is an approximation (pairs are not independent); the exact chance of no match is 49.3% (c1). Demo.tsx computes ALL_MISS from the same constants that draw the ring.

recall.question: A class has 30 students. Which is more likely: some two of them share a birthday, or no two do?
recall.why: 30 students make 435 pairs, and any one of them can match. The chance of a match is about 71%.
